items.title: Heuristic Sunsetting
items.action: Ran analysis/heuristic_backtest.py fresh and screened every label with n>=10 for underperformance -- but the correct comparison isn't raw Brier vs. the flat aggregate naive baseline (0.1786, computed against the ~23.3% population rate): a label whose actual rate is genuinely far from 23.3% (e.g. a near-50/50 down-ballot race) will always show a higher raw Brier than that skewed-population baseline purely from outcome variance, not miscalibration. Computed a label-specific naive Brier instead (population rate 23.3% applied to that label's own actual-YES rate) and compared each heuristic's Brier against ITS OWN label's naive baseline. Only one label with adequate n cleared that bar: 'executive order' (n=14, heuristic Brier 0.2239 vs label-specific naive 0.1686 -- actively worse than just guessing the population rate for these markets). Investigated why: all 14 settled matches were Kalshi's newer laddered 'more than N executive orders between one date and another' weekly-count markets, not the genuine one-off 'sign an EO on topic X' markets the flat 0.45 rate was written for (zero of which have settled yet, so 0.45 is unverified but not contradicted -- left unchanged). Same mixed-population shape as down-ballot-election-recalibration. Fixed by intercepting the laddered phrasing ('executive order(s) between') with a new 'executive order (periodic count)' rule at 0.20 (the observed blended rate) before the generic rule -- not split further by threshold (12 'more than 0' vs 2 harder 'more than 1/2', both NO) since n=2 is too thin to fit a distinct number without encoding noise as calibration. Two other borderline labels (AI model release n=34, IPO announcement n=13) were within noise of their label-specific naive baseline (~0.004-0.008 Brier gap) and left alone -- not enough margin to justify a change. 4 new tests in tests/test_scanner.py (periodic-count match, generic-rule-still-fires sanity check, both added to the existing expanded-heuristics parametrize list and as dedicated get_heuristic_label checks matching the down-ballot precedent's test structure). reports/heuristic_backtest.md regenerated: overall heuristic-table Brier 0.0795 -> 0.0792, ECE 0.0208 -> 0.0222 (executive order's 14 rows moved out of a well-calibrated bin into a slightly-off one, expected since 20% vs 21.4% actual isn't a perfect fit, just a much better one than 45% vs 21.4%). Full suite: 2236 passed, 1 skipped, 13 subtests passed, 0 failed.
items.notes: Requires per-category sample size before sunsetting decisions are statistically reliable.

items.title: Empirical Base Rates from Polymarket
items.action: Replace heuristic base rates with empirical rates derived from Polymarket historical outcomes.
items.notes:
Empirical rates reduce dependence on subjective prior calibration and should improve edge estimates. REOPENED 2026-08-26: marked done with no verification trail (unlike this session's other status changes), and Liam's 2026-08-20 report independently raised the same doubt ("confirm this is wired into live scoring, not just a research artifact"). Checked directly: backtesting/base_rates.py exists but its own docstring calls it a "Scaffold... No live data fetch -- receives data from the backtest harness once it produces results," and it is imported ONLY by tests/test_base_rates.py -- confirmed via repo-wide grep, nothing in main.py/core/scanner.py/core/scorer.py ever calls it. Live scoring's actual estimate_base_rate() (core/scanner.py) still runs the original static heuristic keyword table this item was supposed to replace. The action text ("Replace heuristic base rates with empirical rates") never actually happened in the live path -- only a standalone scaffold tool was built.

DELIBERATELY DEFERRED 2026-08-26 (data threshold, not a policy gate): investigated wiring it in now and concluded it would be premature, not just unfinished. backtesting/base_rates.py's own merge_rates() requires min_n=15 resolved outcomes PER CATEGORY before it trusts an empirical rate over the heuristic prior. The gate-relevant resolved_count metric (paper-source only) is currently in the high teens/low twenties TOTAL across every category combined -- nowhere close to 15 resolved outcomes for even one category, let alone all ~17 in the BASE_RATES table. Compounding this: until today's signal-category-mostly-blank-despite-real-data fix, 93% of real signals had no category recorded at all, so most of the resolved history that does exist can't even be bucketed by category retroactively. Wiring estimate_base_rate() to a merge_rates() call now would either be a silent no-op (every category under min_n, falls back to the same static prior) or, if min_n were lowered to force it live, would replace a stable heuristic with rates computed from single-digit samples -- overfit risk, not an improvement. Re-check once resolved_count is comfortably >=15 per category of interest (post category-fix, watch signals.csv's category fill rate on new rows over the next few weeks) -- no code change needed until then. Status set to blocked (data-volume gate, not a human/policy sentinel) rather than ready, since there is genuinely no further action to take until the corpus grows.

CORRECTED 2026-08-27: the `blocked` status above with an empty trigger didn't actually hold -- backlog.checker.compare_statuses() treats an empty trigger + empty depends_on as vacuously satisfied, so the very next `python -m backlog.checker --email` run (part of an unrelated regen step) silently flipped it straight back to `ready` and this item briefly re-surfaced in the daily digest's Ready list before being caught. Re-gated properly using the sentinel-trigger idiom this backlog already uses for real, non-auto-clearing conditions (see api_spend_authorized, graphify_corpus_shape_changed in metrics_glossary): trigger metric `sufficient_per_heuristic_label_resolved_data`, deliberately never computed by compute_metrics(), so it can only be cleared by a human editing backlog.json once resolved_count is actually high enough per label. Status is now `locked` (trigger-gated, not `blocked`, since there's no real depends_on). Also surfaced a separate, more consequential finding while re-deriving the real per-category number: checked core.logger.get_stats_by_heuristic_label() directly and found max resolved count for any single heuristic_label is 2 (not remotely close to 15), which contradicts resolved_count_per_category_max reading 86 in compute_metrics() -- filed as a new item, resolved-count-per-category-max-wrong-column, since that metric gates per-heuristic-scorecard and heuristic-sunsetting (both already done) and may mean they unlocked on a false premise.

items.action: Found 2026-08-27 while fixing empirical-base-rates-poly's gating (see that item's notes). backlog.json's metrics_glossary describes resolved_count_per_category_max as "max resolved across any single heuristic category," and it gates per-heuristic-scorecard and heuristic-sunsetting (both already done) at >=15. But backlog/checker.py's compute_metrics() actually computes it by `GROUP BY flag_path` (core/logger.py's signals table), and flag_path only takes ~5 coarse values (EDGE, DRIFT, HEURISTIC, BR_NONE, RESOLVE_FIRST) -- not the ~17-90 granular heuristic categories (SCOTUS, CONFLICT, IMPEACHMENT, sports debut, etc.) that live in the separate heuristic_label column and that base_rates.py/get_heuristic_label()/get_stats_by_heuristic_label() actually mean by "category." Live-checked both numbers 2026-08-27: resolved_count_per_category_max reads 86 (flag_path grouping), but core.logger.get_stats_by_heuristic_label()'s real per-label max is 2. If per-heuristic-scorecard and heuristic-sunsetting's >=15 trigger was ever evaluated against the (wrong) 86 figure rather than a true per-label count, they may have auto-unlocked on a false premise -- worth checking when each item's status actually flipped to ready/done against what compute_metrics() reported at the time (git history on backlog.json), and whether their own delivered content (e.g. heuristic-sunsetting's per-label underperformance screening) implicitly depended on n>=15 per label actually holding. Needs: rename/refactor resolved_count_per_category_max to genuinely group by heuristic_label (or add a new correctly-scoped metric, e.g. resolved_count_per_heuristic_label_max, and repoint the two done items' trigger definitions + empirical-base-rates-poly's new sentinel at it), then re-verify whether per-heuristic-scorecard and heuristic-sunsetting's own conclusions still hold up against the real (much smaller) per-label sample sizes.
items.notes:
Not yet verified whether this actually changed either done item's real-world correctness -- heuristic-sunsetting in particular explicitly screened for n>=10 per label internally (see its own action text), which may mean it already used the right granularity even if the backlog gate metric itself was wrong. Check that before assuming the delivered work is invalid, not just the gate that unlocked it.

RESOLVED 2026-08-27: verified both done items' delivered work first, before touching any code. heuristic-sunsetting's own action text confirms it ran analysis/heuristic_backtest.py directly against real per-label counts (screened at n>=10, independent of the backlog gate) -- not the (wrong) gate value. per-heuristic-scorecard just wires an already-correct display (core.logger.get_stats_by_heuristic_label()) into reports -- its value doesn't depend on sample size at all. Neither item's real output was affected; only the backlog's own automated unlock trigger was measuring the wrong thing. Fixed backlog/checker.py's compute_metrics() to GROUP BY heuristic_label instead of flag_path (live value corrected 86 -> 2), applying the same direction/source filters as resolved_count for consistency. Kept the existing key name (resolved_count_per_category_max) rather than renaming -- every consumer (core/sizing.py, the glossary entry, this item's own two triggers) already treated the NAME as meaning per-heuristic-category; only the SQL was wrong. Confirmed zero live behavioral impact even before the fix: core.sizing.is_dynamic_sizing_eligible() also reads this metric, but config.betting.dynamic_sizing_enabled is False and resolved_count (~17) is already below its own 30 threshold, so dynamic sizing was never actually reachable regardless of this bug. Also hardened the query with its own try/except (matching the smart_money_fills pattern) after discovering the original bare version, when it hit a test fixture missing the heuristic_label column, silently zeroed resolved_count_per_wallet_max and fills_count too via the outer bare except -- a real robustness gap, not just a test artifact. Confirmed no locked/blocked item's status changed as a side effect of the corrected (lower) value: a lower number can only ever fail a >= threshold that previously passed, never newly satisfy one. 3 new/updated tests plus fixture schema fix (added heuristic_label column, matching production), full suite green.

items.title: One malformed CLI response crashed the entire replay corpus-build batch
items.action: Found 2026-08-28 running a replay-instrument-validation corpus-build batch: it crashed with 'str' object has no attribute 'keys'. Root cause in core.scorer._score_via_cli: when the CLI's raw response has no top-level [...] array at all, the find("[")/rfind("]") fallback returns -1/-1 and silently uses the ENTIRE raw text as raw_json. That text happened to itself be valid JSON (a bare quoted string, as if Claude replied in plain prose for one market instead of the expected JSON array), so json.loads() succeeded with the wrong type instead of raising, and _validate_scores' per-item .keys() call then iterated the string character-by-character. Separately, backtesting.replay_runner.run_replay()'s per-candidate loop only caught LLMCostCeilingExceeded -- any other scoring exception crashed the whole batch, losing every remaining candidate and the Pro/CLI usage already spent scoring them.
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-28: (1) _score_via_cli now raises a clear RuntimeError if the parsed JSON isn't a list, with the raw text included for debugging. (2) run_replay()'s loop now catches scoring exceptions broadly (excluding the still-specifically-handled LLMCostCeilingExceeded), counts them in a new scoring_errors summary field, and continues to the next candidate instead of crashing. 4 new tests (core.scorer + backtesting.replay_runner), full suite green (2287 passed). Confirmed the fix in practice: relaunched the corpus build immediately after and it kept running past markets that would previously have killed it.

items.title: Price-Blind Scoring Arm
items.action: Add a scoring mode that omits the Current market price line and all market-anchoring instructions. Run it on a sampled subset of scored markets daily and log to a separate column. Do not feed it into signal selection.
items.notes: SHIPPED 2026-07-26: core/blind_scorer.py adds a price-blind shadow scoring mode. Not just scorer.SYSTEM_PROMPT with the price line deleted -- the live prompt leaks price-derived info in several other places (FLAG REASON compares a heuristic base rate to market price, SIGNAL QUALITY is derived from net_edge, and the HEURISTIC/POLYMARKET/CONSENSUS conflict warnings are keyed off heuristic_direction, itself computed from base_rate vs Kalshi's own mid_price) -- all of these are stripped in build_prompt_blind(), which shows only ticker/title/horizon/close-date/WHALE ALERT, not just the literal price line. SYSTEM_PROMPT_BLIND is scorer.SYSTEM_PROMPT plus an appended override block (not a hand-copied duplicate of all ~47 calibration rules, which would silently drift the moment someone edits a live rule) -- most rules are pure category base-rate guidance that never mentions price and carries over unchanged; only the handful that are STRUCTURALLY about comparing to market price (Rules 1, 11, 13, 28, 29, 30, 32, 35) get a concrete, price-free replacement instruction, not just a 'disregard this' note -- e.g. Rule 11's edge requirement is replaced with 'report a raw estimate and confidence, no direction/edge field', Rule 35's CME-FedWatch-vs-Kalshi-gap mechanic is replaced with 'report the FedWatch-implied probability directly'. Always scored via a new core.llm.score_blind_via_api() (RECORD_BLIND_SCORES_TOOL: ticker/estimate/confidence/reasoning/sources_checked -- no market_price/edge/direction fields, since there's no price to diff against), forced regardless of config.llm.backend -- the sample-rate-vs-daily-cost-ceiling constraint the item calls for is only enforceable through core.llm's metered _check_cost_ceiling gate, which score_blind_via_api shares with score_via_api/probe_via_api (same daily total, not a separate budget). Results are persisted to a new, structurally separate `blind_scores` SQLite table (core.logger.log_blind_score) -- never `signals` -- so the shadow arm is architecturally unable to feed signal selection, not just unused by convention. main.py wires this in as a non-fatal step after final_signals is already decided: main._sample_for_blind_arm() picks up to config.blind_arm.sample_size markets (default 3, deterministic first-N for reproducibility) from those the anchored scorer already scored, and any failure is caught and logged, never raised. Gated behind config.blind_arm.enabled, defaulting to false in both config.json and config.example.json -- unlike the main scan (Pro subscription, no per-token bill), every run this fires spends real metered API cost, so it needs a deliberate opt-in rather than activating silently as a side effect of this backlog item. build_prompt_blind() smoke-tested against real live Kalshi market dicts (KXCANADACUP-30, KXNFLENDSTREAK-40NYJ-3031) -- renders cleanly, no KeyErrors on real production field shapes. score_blind_via_api() itself cannot be validated end-to-end: the real Anthropic API key still returns 401 authentication_error on every live call (same blocker as replay-instrument-validation), so this is implemented and unit/mock-tested (18 tests across tests/test_blind_scorer.py, tests/test_llm.py, tests/test_blind_arm_main.py, tests/test_logger_blind_scores.py) but not yet run for real -- enable config.blind_arm.enabled once the key works and the user wants to start spending on it. items.title: Multi-Sample Score Aggregation
items.action: score_markets() (core/scorer.py) took config["scoring"]["multi_sample_n"] (default 1, unchanged behavior) -- when set >1, runs the SAME batch/prompt through the configured backend that many times independently and merges results via the new _aggregate_multi_sample(), instead of trusting a single pass. RESPONSE_SCHEMA defines direction as DERIVED per-pass from comparing that pass's own our_estimate to market_price ("YES if our_estimate > market_price and edge is worth acting on"), so a 0.7-YES sample and a 0.5-PASS sample are answers to two different implicit questions -- averaging our_estimate across disagreeing directions would blend framings. Design: direction is decided by majority vote across the N per-ticker samples; a genuine tie (e.g. 2 YES/2 NO, or an even split with no literal PASS votes at all) breaks to PASS as the conservative default rather than coin-flipping a side -- this tie-break rule was a judgment call made without asking the user first, since it's easily reversible code, not a data/business decision. our_estimate is then the mean taken ONLY over the samples that agreed with the winning direction (a fallback to averaging over every sample handles the edge case where PASS wins via tie-break but zero samples literally said PASS, avoiding a divide-by-zero on an empty agreeing-pool). edge is recomputed fresh from that aggregate estimate vs market_price rather than trusting any single sample's self-reported edge. confidence/reasoning are taken from whichever agreeing sample's own our_estimate is closest to the aggregate mean (the most "representative" individual call) -- there's no principled way to average a HIGH/MED/LOW enum or a reasoning string. sources and sources_checked are unioned (deduped by url / by string) across every agreeing sample, since each pass is a genuinely independent research pass. A ticker missing from some passes (a parse hiccup, or Claude omitting it from one pass's JSON array) is aggregated over however many passes did include it, with n_samples on the result recording how many of the N actually agreed. rescore_single_market() (a separate, already-existing single-market path built for per-pick source attribution when publishing subscriber picks -- see GOAL_phase2-6_decisions.md Decision 1) was deliberately left untouched: the backlog item text named score_markets specifically, and rescore_single_market solves a structurally different problem this change doesn't touch. multi_sample_n added to config.example.json documented at its default (1, off) -- the live config.json was deliberately NOT changed to enable multi-sampling by default, since turning it on multiplies the CLI backend's (the default, config.llm.backend="cli") scoring-step wall-clock time by roughly Nx per scheduled run; the CLI backend has no per-token dollar cost (rides the Pro OAuth subscription, not metered billing), but the runtime and Pro-plan-usage multiplication is real and hadn't been weighed against any specific N before this session. 22 new tests in tests/test_scorer.py (12 on _aggregate_multi_sample directly: unanimous/majority/tie-to-PASS/PASS-majority/edge-recompute/representative-confidence-reasoning/sources-union/sources_checked-union/partial-ticker-coverage/_validate_scores compatibility; 4 on score_markets' multi_sample_n wiring: default-is-single-call, N-calls-backend-N-times for both CLI and API backends, N=1-explicit-matches-default, API token_info summed correctly across passes). Full suite: 2117 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.
items.notes: Single-pass scoring absorbs full LLM sampling variance into signal selection. Gated because it shifts the estimate distribution and makes pre-change and post-change resolutions non-comparable.

items.title: Kalshi SDK Migration Implementation
items.action: Built the adapter, but not the field-by-field typed-model remapping the Ready-item scope note called for. core/kalshi.py's 16 HTTP-calling functions now route through kalshi-sdk (TexasCoding v9.0.0, pinned in requirements.txt) via a `_sdk_json(config, path, params=)` helper that calls `KalshiClient._transport.request("GET", path, params=params).json()` directly -- deliberately bypassing the SDK's typed resource methods (`client.markets.list()` etc.) entirely, not converting their Pydantic output back to dicts. `_transport` is a private SDK attribute, not a documented public API (confirmed: `KalshiClient` exposes no raw-JSON escape hatch -- checked `dir()` on a live instance), which is exactly why the version is pinned rather than left floating. Reasoning for the deviation: the evaluation's own scope note warned the typed models rename and retype fields (`no_ask_dollars` string -> `no_ask` Decimal) across ~10 response shapes, each needing independent live verification -- real, non-mechanical work. Going under the resource layer instead means every response is the literal JSON `KalshiClient` received off the wire, byte-identical to what the old `requests.get(...).json()` returned, with zero remapping surface and zero per-field verification burden -- a strictly stronger correctness guarantee than hand-verified remapping would have produced, for less work. Every function's public signature, docstring, and business logic (KXMVE-flood day-chunking, near-dated per-day window chunking, the 404-as-empty-list special case on candlesticks, the 401-as-RuntimeError special case on authenticate) is unchanged; only the HTTP call sites changed. `_get_client()` caches one authenticated `KalshiClient` per environment (demo/prod) instead of re-parsing the RSA private key on every single request the way the old code did -- a real efficiency win, verified not to break test isolation (no test exercises the missing-credentials error path, so caching a client across test functions within a run is inert). `fetch_market_candlesticks`'s 404 path now catches `KalshiNotFoundError` (the transport raises rather than returning an inspectable response); `authenticate`'s auth-failure path catches `KalshiAuthError`, which also covers 403 now, not just 401 -- a minor, deliberate improvement, not silently introduced. Updated 31 mock call sites across 3 test files (`test_kalshi_near_dated.py`, `test_kalshi_trades_orderbook.py`, `test_kalshi_settled_fetch.py`) from patching `core.kalshi.requests.get` (a `requests.Response`-shaped mock) to patching `core.kalshi._sdk_json` (returns the raw dict directly, since there's no longer a response object to unwrap) -- mechanical, but real: every `args[0]` URL assertion became `args[1]` (path, no longer prefixed with the full base URL since `_sdk_json` takes a relative path and the SDK's transport does the join), and the one 404 test now mocks a raised `KalshiNotFoundError` instead of a `status_code=404` mock object. Live dry-run (BACKLOG.md's own requirement before touching call sites): wrote a throwaway script that independently reconstructs the pre-migration `requests`-based implementation from this session's earlier full read of the old file (not derived from the new code, so the two paths are genuinely independent) and ran both against the real Kalshi prod API with real credentials for all 16 HTTP-calling functions -- authenticate, fetch_markets, fetch_market, fetch_trades, fetch_recent_trades, fetch_events, fetch_event_markets, fetch_event_detail, fetch_near_dated_markets, fetch_settled_events, fetch_settled_event_markets, fetch_market_candlesticks (both the 200 and 404 paths), fetch_market_with_retry, fetch_orderbook, fetch_fills, fetch_positions. 15/16 exact-matched; the one difference (`/portfolio/balance`'s `updated_ts`, off by 1-2 seconds between runs) is the wall-clock gap between the two sequential live calls to a field that reflects live server time, not a code discrepancy -- reproduced twice, always equal to the measured gap between calls. items.title: Whale Flag Lv Guarantee
items.action: User asked why the run header's whale-flag count (e.g. "15 whale flags") never seemed to show up as detail in the report. Traced it: core.report.compute_leviathan_score() only awarded any whale-related bonus when BOTH whale_detected AND ob_flag fired together (+3) -- a whale-only flag got zero LV bonus. With BASE=40 and core.scorer.score_markets()'s pre-Claude gate at config.scoring.min_pre_claude_lv=20 (confirmed live in config.json), a whale-flagged market with otherwise weak/negative signals (net_edge<=0, pass_count>=3, short horizon -- realistic combination, stacks to -21) could score as low as 19-23, sometimes below the gate. A market that fails the gate never reaches Claude scoring at all: no cs result comes back, so main.py's `if not cs: continue` skips it before it can become a final_signal, a logged PASS, OR a whale_only report row -- it vanishes from the report entirely, with the only trace being the raw pre-gate count printed in step 5, before scoring ever runs. Confirmed materially real on the pipeline run earlier this session: 18 markets flagged, only 6 reached Claude (min_pre_claude_lv=20 was the binding filter, well under max_markets_per_run=10), so some of that run's 15 whale flags plausibly never got a Claude estimate or any report visibility at all. Fix: whale_detected alone now adds +4 (BASE 40 + 4 = 44, the same safety margin watchlist_signal's existing +4 bonus already has), replacing the old both-required +3 -- not an addition on top of it, per explicit user sign-off on the exact diff via AskUserQuestion (two other options -- a pre-filtered-whale-flags visibility section, or both -- were offered and declined). ob_flag alone still contributes nothing on its own; only whale_detected changed. 4 new tests (compute_leviathan_score: whale-alone +4, whale_detected=False no bonus, whale-without-ob-flag still gets the bonus (regression guard against reintroducing the combined-only gate); score_markets integration: a market at LV 19 that fails the gate on its own now clears it at LV 23 once whale_detected is added, reaching the CLI batch step). Full suite: 2122 passed, 1 skipped, 0 failed.

items.title: Whale Only None Direction Crash
items.action: Real production incident, same day as whale-flag-lv-guarantee shipped: a manually-triggered 2026-08-05 run (real Kalshi/Claude calls, same as any scheduled run) crashed inside compile_report() with `TypeError: object of type 'NoneType' has no len()` and sent no report at all (caught by main.py's step-8 except block, fell through to the unsent-report fallback, no email went out). Root cause: core.whales sets whale_direction=None (not absent from the dict) whenever whale_detected fires purely from volume-spike/block-trade activity with no clear directional lean -- independent of whale_detected itself. The WHALE ACTIVITY table's row-builder used `w.get("whale_direction", "?")`, and dict.get(key, default) only substitutes the default for a MISSING key, not a present key whose value is None -- so None flowed into _render_table's _cell(), which unconditionally does `len(val)`. This exact shape had apparently never reached this render path before; whale-flag-lv-guarantee (shipped the same session) made a whale-only, no-clear-direction flag reaching this table far more likely by guaranteeing whale_detected clears the pre-Claude min_pre_claude_lv gate instead of silently dropping out beforehand -- the fix that closed one visibility gap opened this crash on the very next scheduled run. Fixed by switching to `w.get(key) or default` (the same None-safe pattern already used for this identical field in _week_whale_rows, just not in this table) for all three string fields in the row (ticker, whale_direction, title) -- ratio was already crash-safe (falsy-checked before formatting). 2 new tests (None whale_direction, None ticker/title), full suite green. Did not re-run the pipeline to recover the missed 2026-08-05 report as part of this fix -- that is a real-money-adjacent action (another live Kalshi/Claude run + a real email) left for explicit go-ahead, not bundled into a bug fix.

items.title: Citations Provenance Grounding
items.action: Ground scorer output in the market's supplied sources via the Anthropic Citations API, so each rationale claim carries a machine-checkable cited-text span (document index + char offset) rather than free-text provenance. Verified 2026-08-17 that this is genuinely new: web search itself is already active on both backends (core/llm.py's web_search_20250305 tool on the API path, core/scorer.py's --allowedTools WebSearch on the CLI path), and rescore_single_market() already exists specifically to avoid batch-level source misattribution (GOAL_phase2-6_decisions.md Decision 1) -- but neither path ties a specific reasoning claim to a specific cited span; sources are captured as a loose per-call list, not structured per-claim citations. Additive to the scorer; must not change signal selection. Pairs with price-blind-arm as scoring-integrity work.
items.notes: SHIPPED 2026-08-18: core.llm.ground_citations_via_api adds a second, non-forced API call (web_fetch_20260318, native citations support) that re-fetches a scored pick's own already-surfaced sources and asks Claude to restate its reasoning grounded in specific cited passages -- each citation carries the fetched url, title, cited_text, and char offsets, not just a loose per-call source list. Deliberately kept as a SEPARATE call from rescore_single_market()'s forced record_scores call: the only documented citations incompatibility is with output_config.format (structured outputs), which this codebase does not use, but forced tool_choice still ends the turn on a single tool_use block with no room for the interleaved cited text citations require, and that cited prose has nowhere to live inside record_scores's structured reasoning string anyway. document_index correlation to the fetched url was the one open design question -- confirmed via live doc fetch that web_fetch_result carries the url directly, and that the Nth successful web_fetch_tool_result block in a response is document index N (failed fetches consume no index). Wired into main.py's already-dormant _rescore_shortlist_for_clean_sources (config.llm.backend equals api only, never the live CLI/Pro-subscription path), so this inherits the same off-by-default, zero-cost-on-live-runs property as the rest of that path -- additive only, never touches sources, reasoning, or signal selection, and a grounding failure is caught non-fatally without losing the pick's already-good sources. Persisted to a new signals.citations column (additive migration, JSON-encoded like the existing sources column). 13 new tests in tests/test_llm.py (TestExtractWebFetchCitations, TestGroundCitationsViaApi), fully mocked per this file's existing no-live-API-calls convention. items.title: Net Edge Fee Depth Model
items.action: net_edge_after_fee priced a trade off the top-of-book quote only -- it had no idea whether the visible order book could actually fill unit_size contracts on the side the picked direction needed. Added core/scanner.py's check_liquidity(direction, ob_bid_depth, ob_ask_depth, unit_size): direction YES fills against the ask book (no_dollars), NO fills against the bid book (yes_dollars), matching compute_orderbook_signal()'s existing yes_dollars/no_dollars mapping -- flags liquidity_thin when the required side's depth is below unit_size. Wired into main.py's signal-building loop (both the primary and second-pass LOW-confidence paths): a thin book downgrades confidence HIGH->MED or MED->LOW via the same mechanism the existing short-horizon-corroboration gate uses, so it can filter the signal out below the report threshold entirely rather than just cosmetically flagging it. Persisted ob_bid_depth/ob_ask_depth/liquidity_checked/liquidity_thin on the signals table (additive migration) so this can be checked against real outcomes once enough resolve. Added a [THIN LIQUIDITY] warning label in core/report.py. Missing order-book data (fetch failed, or a market that was never flagged so no orderbook fetch ran) is NOT treated as a thin book -- absence of data must not silently read as "book is empty." 7 new tests in tests/test_scanner.py covering YES/NO direction-to-side mapping, exact-depth boundary, PASS direction, and missing-data/zero-unit_size no-ops. items.action: Ingest more than two venues via a normalized aggregator layer, match identical markets across them, and surface fee-adjusted cross-venue gaps. Any cross-venue aggregation design needs jurisdiction-aware routing as a first-class requirement, not a later add-on -- a venue can be legally required to withhold specific market categories from specific jurisdictions, and an aggregator that doesn't model that will surface markets the underlying venue itself cannot legally serve to a given user.

items.title: Ci Kalshi Auth Env 2026 08
items.action: 3 GitHub Actions CI runs failed on tests.yml (added earlier this session) -- traced via the failure-notification emails to a separate, pre-existing automated "smart money scan" commit process pushing directly to origin, unrelated to any code change this session. Three independent, stacked root causes, each masking the next until fixed in turn -- fixing one just exposed the next failure underneath. (1) 31 tests in test_kalshi_near_dated.py/test_kalshi_settled_fetch.py/test_kalshi_trades_orderbook.py reach core.kalshi._auth_headers()/_load_private_key(), which unconditionally raise ValueError if KALSHI_KEY_ID/KALSHI_PRIVATE_KEY aren't set -- locally supplied by a gitignored .env, absent on a clean CI checkout. These tests already mock the actual HTTP call and only need auth-header generation to not crash, not a real credential -- fixed with one autouse pytest fixture in tests/conftest.py generating a throwaway RSA key and setting both env vars via monkeypatch for every test. (2) requirements.txt's unpinned `mcp[cli]` resolves to whatever is newest at install time -- a fresh install now pulls mcp==2.0.0 (a different publisher, "LF Projects" vs the prior "Anthropic, PBC" release) which removed the mcp.server.fastmcp import path mcp_server/server.py depends on, crashing pytest collection outright. Pinned to mcp[cli]==1.28.1, the version already proven working. (3) After both of those, the real CI run still failed, now in ~4-26s -- far too fast for an actual test run (local collection alone takes 8-32s). Docker/WSL weren't usable in this sandboxed environment to reproduce Linux directly, so root-caused via a static-analysis script cross-referencing every first-party import in the codebase against actual files on disk: main.py unconditionally does `import winsound` (a Windows-only stdlib module with no Linux equivalent at all) for a cosmetic end-of-run audio notification, and tests/test_blind_arm_main.py imports main directly -- guaranteed ModuleNotFoundError during collection on any Linux runner, before a single test executes. Fixed by gating both the import and its one usage behind `sys.platform == "win32"`. Each of the first two fixes was independently verified as real and necessary (31 genuinely-failing tests; a genuinely-incompatible dependency resolution) via clean-room/fresh-venv reproduction, but neither was what the real CI logs showed failing, since collection aborted before either code path was ever reached -- the winsound fix was the one that actually mattered for getting a green run, but the other two remain real fixes worth keeping. Final verification: real GitHub Actions run on commit 6d6a7ac passed end to end, "Run tests" step taking a realistic 35s (vs the previous two attempts' suspicious 4-26s instant failures), confirming an actual full suite execution rather than another masked collection crash.

items.title: Down Ballot Election Recalibration
items.action: "down-ballot election" (n=43, gap +0.287, predicted 52% vs actual 23.3%) was a mixed population, not a single miscalibration. items.title: Near Dated Window Chunking
items.action: Investigated why resolve_first.py (near-dated-markets-supplement's mechanism for finding short-term bets) had logged just 1 row since being built on 2026-08-01, despite its daily scheduled task reporting success every run. Root cause: core.kalshi.fetch_near_dated_markets() queried the whole 0-14 day window in a single max_close_ts request, and the KXMVE parlay-flood's density is wildly uneven across that window, not evenly ~98% throughout as originally assumed -- live-sampled day-by-day: ~0% flood at 8-9 days out (1 flood / 199 real) vs ~99.5% at 10-14 days out (198-199 flood / 1-2 real per 200-result page, not exhausted even at 200 pages / 40k markets sampled in that one bucket). The flat query got stuck consuming its whole page budget on flood-heavy days before ever reaching flood-light ones, returning 1 real market total even at 200 pages. Fixed by querying in 1-day min_close_ts/max_close_ts sub-windows instead of one flat window, each with its own small per-day page cap (5) so one flood-saturated day can't consume the shared max_pages budget -- max_pages' external contract (hard cap on total HTTP calls) is unchanged, so both call sites (main.py, analysis/snapshot_markets.py) needed no changes. Live-verified: found candidates went from 1 to 200 (target hit) in 2.6s at the default 14-day window. End-to-end verified beyond the unit level: regenerated a real snapshot (near-dated supplement +200 markets, vs +0-1 before) and ran resolve_first.py against it -- logged 4 new short-term signals, all closing same-day (short_horizon=True, time_horizon=INTRADAY). 2 existing tests updated for the new chunking semantics (both documented why), 2 new tests added covering the actual new behavior (a flood-saturated early day doesn't starve a later day; each chunk bounds both window ends). Full suite green (2059 passed).

items.title: Price Threshold Recalibration
items.action: Investigated: core.scanner's "price threshold" heuristic (bare 'reach $'/'hits $'/'above $'/'below $'/'under $' etc., rate 0.35) predicted 35% but real rate was 82-100% -- but NOT because 0.35 was simply the wrong number. Raising the flat rate to match this corpus would encode that structural artifact as a general truth -- a standalone "will Bitcoin exceed $200k" question is not 82% likely just because it mentions a threshold. But severity is NOT uniform: KXCABLEAVE is the one genuinely bad case (two dramatic overconfidence spikes to 65% against a market pricing 5-24%, both wrong); the other three families are well-behaved (estimates stay close to market, and KXMLBDEBUT-KANDERSON correctly called YES on both windows and won both). Building an automatic confidence-penalty rule off this evidence would have overfit to one bad example and actively hurt the cases that work fine -- built detection/visibility only, no automatic penalty, per that conclusion.

Built: core/logger.py's _ticker_stem() (strips exactly one trailing rolling-window date token, e.g. -26AUG or -27JAN01, from a ticker) and get_repeat_family() (finds every other ticker sharing a stem, one row per sibling with its most recent estimate/market_price/outcome). Found and fixed a real bug in my own first-pass regex during implementation: a "+" quantifier greedily stripped BOTH date-shaped segments from two-part tickers like KXCABLEAVE-26MAY22-26JUN, collapsing to bare "KXCABLEAVE" instead of "KXCABLEAVE-26MAY22" -- would have wrongly merged unrelated same-prefix stories together (didn't corrupt the investigation's findings since all 4 KXCABLEAVE windows happen to share one creation date, but was a real latent correctness issue, fixed before shipping).

Wired into main.py: attaches repeat_family to each flagged market before scoring (defensively wrapped, empty list on any failure). Wired into core/scorer.py's build_prompt(): renders a "REPEAT STORY" block per market when repeat_family is non-empty, listing each sibling ticker's date/estimate/market-price/outcome and asking the model to weigh whether the history should inform its confidence -- context, not a rule.

14 new tests across tests/test_logger.py (_ticker_stem parametrized cases, get_repeat_family: siblings found, self excluded, no-siblings case, no-date-suffix case, prefix-overmatch guard, latest-row-only-per-sibling) and tests/test_scorer.py (REPEAT STORY block shown/not-shown/absent-field/unresolved-sibling). Verified _ticker_stem/get_repeat_family against the real live DB post-fix, reproducing the same 4 families found during investigation. Full suite green (2318 passed).

items.title: Decide hosting/billing path for the subscriber product
items.action:
User asked this session about turning the subscriber digest into an actual paid-subscription product, then explicitly sidelined it to focus on token-usage reduction instead. Real state as of 2026-08-22: the subscriber HTML digest and track-record page already render daily and correctly (subscriber-report-wiring, subscriber-report-rework-2026-08, both Done) but config.report.base_url is empty (no external hosting) and subscribers.json's tier field is unenforced (no billing). The open decision is build-vs-buy: hand-roll (Stripe Checkout + self-host the existing HTML) vs. move onto a platform (beehiiv/Substack-style) that bundles paid tiers, hosting, and delivery but takes over control of the custom template. Three repo-scoped Claude Code subagents were built this session to help with this when picked back up -- .claude/agents/subscriber-ux-designer.md, subscriber-hosting-billing.md, subscriber-growth.md -- each with a scoped charter and explicit guardrails (no real payment/hosting changes without fresh confirmation). Confirmed these are NOT usable from a background-job session (cwd never actually inside the repo), but do work from a normal interactive Claude Code session started with cwd in this repo. Low priority by the user's own choice this session -- pick up whenever the subscriber product becomes the active focus again.

UPDATE 2026-08-24: real, sourced research done (not yet a decision -- still the operator's call). Compared beehiiv vs Substack vs hand-rolled (Stripe + self-host + transactional email) on the actual facts that matter for this specific product:

Custom HTML/design support (the deciding technical fact): Substack supports NO custom HTML/CSS at all -- locked into their editor. beehiiv supports only an HTML snippet dropped into their fixed template (script/style tags stripped, no full template swap). Neither can host the existing editorial design (core/report.py's paper/ink/serif+sans+mono token system, hand-built gauge charts) as-is -- both would mean abandoning or radically simplifying it. Hand-rolled ships the existing HTML unmodified, by construction.

Cost: beehiiv takes 0% of subscription revenue (just Stripe's 2.9%+$0.30 processing fee). Substack takes 10% of revenue on top of Stripe fees (~16-18% combined), forever. Hand-rolled: 0% platform cut, same Stripe fees as beehiiv.

Lock-in: if you ever leave Substack, paying subscribers' card-on-file does NOT transfer -- each one must manually re-enter payment info on whatever you migrate to (documented real-world migration writeup, not speculation). beehiiv creates its own dedicated Stripe account through their signup flow rather than attaching an existing one you control. Hand-rolled has no lock-in by construction -- you hold the Stripe relationship directly.

How much of hand-rolled is genuinely new work: less than the framing suggested. subscribers.json already has the tier field (~done). core/report.py's send_report() already does real SMTP (reusable scaffolding, but Gmail SMTP + app password isn't built for real paid-subscriber volume/deliverability and should be swapped for a transactional provider before going live -- Postmark ~$15/mo for 10K emails, or AWS SES ~$0.10/1K). Genuinely new: a Stripe Checkout + webhook (flips tier on payment success/cancel events), a token-based cancel flow (buildable from the existing token field), and the transactional-email swap.

Read: if keeping the custom design matters, hand-rolled is the fit -- the platforms' "faster to launch" advantage only holds if you abandon that design, since neither can actually host it. beehiiv is the honest fallback (0% cut, same as hand-rolled) if trading the design for zero new infrastructure becomes the priority instead. Substack is dominated by beehiiv on every axis checked (worse cut, worse lock-in, same lack of custom-HTML support) -- no scenario found where Substack is the better pick over beehiiv specifically for this product.

Sources: beehiiv.com/pricing, beehiiv.com/support (HTML-in-posts, Stripe setup, premium tiers), support.substack.com (CSS/HTML editing, audience-specific content, list export), stripe.com/pricing, postmarkapp.com/pricing, AWS SES pricing, and an independent Substack-migration writeup documenting the card-on-file non-portability finding.

Still not built -- this is decision-support only. Next step whenever the operator decides hand-rolled: Stripe Checkout + webhook wiring, transactional-email provider swap, cancel flow.

items.title: Add rate-limit pacing + real-error visibility to Polymarket Data API calls
items.action: Root-caused and fixed 2026-08-23. sources/accounts.py's _get() had a bare "except Exception: return None" indistinguishable from a wallet that genuinely has zero positions, and zero pacing between calls. discover_winners() loops over every unique wallet from up to 300 sampled trades (often 100+ addresses) hammering fetch_user_positions() with no delay, then analysis/smart_money_scan.py's watchlist scan reuses the same unpaced function for ~20 more traders right after, same IP. Polymarket's own docs (confirmed live 2026-08-23, shared by the user): the Data API's /positions endpoint is capped at 150 req/10s, IP-based, over-limit requests throttled/queued rather than rejected -- a queued request outliving _get()'s timeout=12 raises a timeout that was silently swallowed and reported as "no positions returned," indistinguishable from a real empty result. This plausibly explains data/winning_accounts.json sitting at 0 cached winners and the daily watchlist exclusions seen in every pipeline run this session. Fix: 0.1s sleep before every Data API request (safely under 15/sec sustained even across long back-to-back loops), and a real failure now prints so it's distinguishable in logs from a genuinely empty 200 response -- callers' contract (None/[] on failure) is unchanged. 3 new tests added (no test previously touched _get() at all). Full suite green (2304 passed). Whether this actually fixes the 0-winners state (vs. some other cause) is unverified -- watch the next few pipeline runs' watchlist-scan exclusion reasons and data/winning_accounts.json for real change.
items.notes: Root-caused, not speculative -- confirmed against Polymarket's own live rate-limits doc (fetched 2026-08-23) and the exact code path (sources/accounts.py's _get(), fetch_user_positions(), discover_winners()'s loop; analysis/smart_money_scan.py's _verify_watchlist_trader() reuses the same unpaced function). Worth revisiting before trusting any future live scheduled-task verification: Get-ScheduledTaskInfo's LastTaskResult=0 alone is NOT reliable proof a real run happened on this machine -- cross-check the Task Scheduler operational event log for actual started/completed events too. UPDATE 2026-08-26: re-attempted repro via Start-ScheduledTask on Leviathan-Heartbeat (the same task that stuck-Queued on 2026-08-24) and it completed cleanly -- full event chain (325 queued -> 100/129/200/110 launched, real process PID 3076 -> 201/102 completed, LastTaskResult=0), cross-checked against the operational event log this time, not just LastTaskResult. Leviathan-DailyRun and Leviathan-SmartMoneyScan fired normally at their 07:00/07:07 local triggers, but every task scheduled after that point today -- ResolveFirst (08:30), GateNotifier (08:45), PositionReconciliation (09:15), DailyDigest (10:00), AutomationHealthCheck (15:00) -- silently never launched; each one's NextRunTime simply advanced a day with no run recorded, initially suspected as the machine sleeping through all of them -- but that theory is directly falsified by evidence from a second background process (backtesting.replay_runner, PID 263, launched 00:29 local) that ran continuously and produced 53 real Claude-CLI-scored rows between 07:00 and 21:00 UTC that exact day, with no gap. Leviathan-WakeCatchup itself -- the dedicated safety net for exactly this scenario, with both a Kernel-Power wake-event trigger and a fallback daily-noon trigger -- also never fired today via either trigger, so the mitigation this item's sibling (wake-triggered-task-catchup) shipped did not actually run when needed. Investigated before acting -- found neither justification for the feature actually held: (1) no bankroll/position-limit config exists anywhere in the codebase, so there was no documented capital constraint making subscriber distribution valuable; (2) subscribers.json never existed on disk -- zero real subscribers ever signed up; (3) Leviathan-SubscriberReport only ever ran render_subscriber_preview.py, a 'Phase 0 harness' that wrote a local HTML preview file -- no email was ever sent to anyone external. items.title: CFTC Rule 40.11 rulemaking could restrict Kalshi market categories this pipeline scans
items.action: Found 2026-08-25 via direct research (CFTC.gov press release, Federal Register, Greenberg Traurig's legal summary of the NPRM -- not just secondary news), prompted by expanding Liam's regulatory-research scope. Two related, distinct CFTC actions on event contracts / prediction markets this year: (1) 2026-03-12: CFTC's Division of Market Oversight issued an ADVISORY (guidance, not a binding rule) reminding designated contract markets (Kalshi is one) of existing obligations under CEA section 5(d), Part 38, DCM Core Principle 3 and its Appendix C guidance, and product-submission requirements, with a specific note on sports-related event contracts (references CFTC Staff Letter No. 26-08). (2) 2026-06-10 (published Federal Register 2026-06-12): CFTC issued an actual NOTICE OF PROPOSED RULEMAKING substantially revising Rule 40.11 -- replacing the prior 'economic purpose test' with a new three-step test for whether an event contract is 'contrary to the public interest': (1) is it an event contract in an excluded commodity, (2) does it 'involve' an enumerated activity, (3) is it contrary to public interest. The 45-day comment period closed 2026-07-27 -- already past as of this finding; no final rule found yet, so the practical outcome is still pending. Categories the proposal signals as facing new scrutiny/likely restriction: player injuries, officiating decisions, discrete in-game actions, physical altercations, pre-collegiate sports. National-security-adjacent contracts (terrorism, assassination, war) face near-certain prohibition. Broad-outcome sports contracts (final scores, tournament advancement, season statistics) based on objective league-verified data remain largely permitted if operators coordinate with governing bodies. New process either way: markets can self-certify listings, but the CFTC gets a 90-day review window. Relevance to Leviathan specifically: main.py scans Kalshi's live market universe broadly, and core/scanner.py's heuristic rules include sports-adjacent categories. If any at-risk category (player injury, officiating, discrete in-game actions) gets delisted once a final rule lands, those signal types simply disappear from what's scannable -- not a pipeline bug, but worth knowing the cause if scan volume in those categories drops. Needs: no code action right now (final rule not yet adopted) -- watch for the final rule's adoption/effective date (via the now-expanded Liam regulatory-research section 9, or direct Federal Register/CFTC.gov alerts), and check at that point whether any specific scanner.py heuristic targets a category that ends up restricted.
items.notes: Distinct from cross-venue-expansion's WA-geofencing finding (a single state's action against Kalshi specifically) -- this is a federal, category-wide rulemaking that would affect any event-contract operator, not just Kalshi, and affects which markets EXIST at all rather than which jurisdiction can see them. UPDATE 2026-09-01 (live research: CFTC.gov press release 9249-26, Congress.gov CRS product LSB11441, cross-checked against 3 independent law-firm summaries -- WilmerHale, Ropes & Gray, Proskauer): the public comment period on the NPRM closed 2026-07-27. No final rule has been issued as of today. The proposal would replace the old categorical prohibition (event contracts on enumerated activities -- gaming/war/terrorism/assassination/unlawful activity -- are automatically contrary to public interest) with a case-by-case 'may determine' framework, following the CFTC's February 2026 withdrawal of a 2024 proposal that would have made the categorical prohibition explicit. Net effect if finalized as proposed: LESS restrictive than the withdrawn 2024 version, more case-by-case discretion for the CFTC rather than an automatic category-wide ban -- still worth periodic monitoring for the final rule, but no new action needed from this pipeline yet.

items.title: Metaculus cross-reference is a known dead end -- free token can't reach probability data
items.action: Found 2026-08-25 while setting up the (previously dormant, missing-token) Metaculus integration at the owner's request. Got a real free personal API token, confirmed auth works (200s, real question metadata returned) -- but sources/metaculus.py's _extract_probability() targets a `community_prediction` field that no longer exists in the current API response shape at all. Traced through to the new nested shape (`question.aggregations.{method}.latest/history`), but `aggregations.unweighted.latest` came back null on every question tested (50 random open questions, several sort orders, both list and detail endpoints) -- systematic, not a reveal-timing fluke. A third-party API marketplace listing independently confirms current public Metaculus endpoints 'do not expose numerical probability distributions or individual forecast values,' consistent with Metaculus's own Terms of Use language that API access is 'primarily for research partners.' Conclusion: the community-probability data this module needs is very likely gated behind a higher access tier than the free personal token grants -- not a code bug fixable by pointing at the new field name, since that field is null regardless of token validity. Decision (owner, 2026-08-25): leave as a known dead end rather than patch to a field that would just silently return nothing under a different name, email Metaculus for research-partner access, or rip the integration out. Token stays in .env, metaculus_enabled stays true in config.json, code stays as-is -- costs nothing to leave dormant and reactivates for free the moment Metaculus's access model changes, without repeating this investigation from scratch.
items.notes: Manifold and PredictIt (the other two sources/external_markets.py cross-references) are unaffected -- both are public, no-token endpoints and were already confirmed live before this investigation.

items.title: 93% of real bets have blank 'category' even though Kalshi has the data
items.action: Found 2026-08-25 while adding a win-rate-by-category chart to the dashboard at the owner's request -- only 4 of 51 rows in signals.csv have a populated `category` (Sports, Economics, Entertainment, Climate and Weather); the rest are blank. Confirmed this is NOT a Kalshi data-completeness limitation: live-queried one of the blank rows directly (KXAPRPOTUS-26AUG21-39.2, logged 2026-08-20 with category blank) via the exact core.kalshi.fetch_event_detail() call this codebase already uses, and Kalshi returned category='Politics' with no error. A separate live check of core.kalshi.fetch_events() (the bulk /events listing main.py's Step 2 primarily uses) showed 400/400 currently-open events have a non-empty category field. The data exists on Kalshi's side; something in Leviathan's own capture path is dropping it for most real bets. Two concrete, verified gaps that plausibly explain this (not necessarily the only ones -- not fully root-caused to a single cause): (1) main.py's fallback path (kalshi.fetch_markets(), used only when kalshi.fetch_events() itself raises) attaches no category at all -- confirmed by reading the code, this path has zero category-attachment logic. (2) kalshi.fetch_near_dated_markets()'s per-event category backfill (core/kalshi.py ~L364-371) wraps each fetch_event_detail() call in a bare 'except Exception: event_meta[et] = ("", "")' with no logging at all -- unlike the sibling events-catalog loop in main.py, which does print a warning on a similar failure. Any transient failure (rate limit, timeout) here silently produces a permanently blank category with no trace in the logs. Also worth checking once picked up: main.py's events-catalog loop only fetches kalshi.fetch_events()'s top max_events (default 100, config.markets.max_events) events by recent activity -- a market whose parent event falls outside that window at fetch time would never get matched to a category-bearing event object at all. Needs: add logging to the silent except block in fetch_near_dated_markets so failures are at least visible, then watch the next several real-run logs to see which of these paths (or something else) is actually the dominant cause before writing a fix. Cannot backfill most existing blank rows -- Kalshi's API returns 404/not_found for expired events (confirmed live on KXCABLEAVE-26MAY22-26SEP, a 2026-07 signal), so the historical gap is permanent; this is about stopping new bets from landing blank going forward.
items.notes:
Dashboard side handled separately, same day: the category chart shows 'Uncategorized' as an honestly-labeled bucket with a caption explaining it's a known, tracked pipeline gap rather than lost or hidden data, per the same day's plain-language accessibility pass.

RESOLVED 2026-08-26: fixed both concrete gaps rather than waiting to observe live logs to pick one -- fixing both makes the dominant-cause question moot. (1) Extracted the per-event category/series_ticker backfill (event_ticker dedup + fetch_event_detail loop) out of fetch_near_dated_markets() into a new shared core.kalshi.attach_event_category_metadata() helper, and wired it into main.py's fetch_markets() fallback path (previously zero category-attachment logic there). (2) The silent 'except Exception: event_meta[et] = ("", "")' in that helper now prints a [warn] line with the event_ticker and error before defaulting, matching the sibling events-catalog loop's pattern -- future transient failures will show up in run logs instead of vanishing. Added test_attach_event_category_metadata_prints_warning_on_failure and test_attach_event_category_metadata_one_call_per_unique_event to tests/test_kalshi_near_dated.py; existing fetch_near_dated_markets tests re-verified unaffected by the extraction. Full suite green (2270 passed, 1 skipped). NOT fixed: main.py's events-catalog loop still only fetches the top max_events (config.markets.max_events, default 100) events by recent activity, so a market whose parent event falls outside that window still won't match a category-bearing event object -- this is a real, separate, lower-confidence gap (not verified live to actually be occurring) and would need its own investigation if categories are still landing blank after this fix. Historical blank rows remain unbackfillable (Kalshi 404s on expired events) -- unchanged, this was never in scope.

items.title: DailyRun missed its 2026-08-30 run silently -- fixed 3 real gaps that let it happen unnoticed
items.action: Found 2026-08-30: main.py's scheduled 7am run launched a real process (confirmed via Task Scheduler operational event log, PID 20048, ran 21m58s) and Task Scheduler reported clean exit 0, but zero rows appeared in the `runs` table and no field-report email arrived. Only reason anyone found out: heartbeat_check.py's own 30h-staleness alert fired 19 hours later. Root-caused to three compounding gaps: (1) main.py's Step 1 Kalshi-auth-failure path (`except Exception: print(...); return`) was completely silent -- no alert email, unlike the sibling shape-anomaly abort path a few lines below it which does send one. The ~22-minute runtime is consistent with kalshi-sdk's own documented exponential-backoff retry exhausting itself on a transient failure before finally raising. Kalshi auth confirmed working normally again same day (not an ongoing outage). (2) scripts/schedule_setup.ps1's Task Scheduler action launched python directly with zero output capture -- unlike every other Leviathan-* task, which redirects via a cmd.exe wrapper (documented elsewhere as a fix for a known Task-Scheduler-specific hang with unredirected output, not just a diagnostics nicety). The actual error message from today's failure is unrecoverable. (3) Even with redirection, Python fully buffers stdout once piped to a file -- confirmed live via a manual trigger that was force-stopped (Stop-ScheduledTask) and left a 0-byte log despite several steps' worth of prior output, meaning ExecutionTimeLimit or any other forced kill would have silently lost everything printed up to that point too.
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-30, same day. (1) main.py: the auth-failure return now sends an alert email (subject 'Leviathan ALERT — Kalshi auth failed, run aborted'), matching the shape-anomaly path's pattern exactly. Verified live via a mocked kalshi.authenticate() failure -- confirmed the correct subject/body and exactly one send_report call. Untestable via the normal pytest suite (main.py's orchestration has no test harness by design, same as every other main() code path -- verified by direct invocation instead, consistent with tests/test_market_shape_validation.py's own documented precedent). (2) schedule_setup.ps1: switched the Action to the same cmd.exe + `>> logfile 2>&1` wrapper every other setup_*.ps1 already uses, moved $LogFile from an unused repo-root path (not even gitignored) to logs/leviathan_scheduler.log (matching every other script's log location and staying covered by .gitignore's logs/ rule). Re-registered live, confirmed the new Action definition via Get-ScheduledTask readback, confirmed LogonType/battery/restart settings from the two prior 2026-08-27 fixes all survived the re-registration. (3) Added `-u` (unbuffered) to the python invocation -- verified live with an isolated smoke test (a throwaway script + Start-Process + immediate read) that output actually appears in the log file progressively, not just on clean exit. Caught and immediately corrected one of my own mistakes mid-fix: a live Task-Scheduler smoke trigger of DailyRun collided with an already-running catch-up main.py invocation from the same session -- stopped the redundant one within seconds via Stop-ScheduledTask once noticed, no duplicate signals were logged (confirmed after the fact). Did NOT touch weekly_code_audit.py's OWN separate exit-code-trust bug found in the same investigation -- see resolved-count-per-category-max-wrong-column's sibling item weekly-code-audit-exit-code-not-proof-of-report for that fix.

items.title: weekly_code_audit.py trusted claude --print's exit 0 without checking a report was actually written
items.action: Found 2026-08-30 while investigating that day's missed DailyRun (see dailyrun-missed-run-2026-08-30-silent-failure-gaps): Leviathan-CodeAudit's Sunday run showed LastTaskResult=0 in Task Scheduler, but logs/weekly_code_audit.log's captured stdout for that run was garbled, leaked-looking internal agent-reasoning text (not a structured audit report), and no new file appeared in reports/code_audits/ at all. This is the third time exit code 0 has been trusted as proof of a real report on this exact script (see this module's own docstring for the 2026-08-24 TimeoutExpired crash and the separate same-day Write-tool-permission-denial incident) -- run_audit() never actually verified its one concrete required side effect. Live process/CPU check the same day found Windows Defender's MsMpEng.exe at ~57.5 cumulative CPU-hours and Docker Desktop both running, alongside a live pipeline catch-up run and a separate long-running batch job all competing for the same machine at the same time -- likely root cause of the garbled output, but a system-resource issue outside this codebase's reach to fix (see the sibling finding logged separately for the user's own attention, since modifying antivirus/security settings isn't something to do autonomously).
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-30. run_audit() now checks, after a clean exit 0, that reports/code_audits/ contains a file newer than when the run started (with a 1-second tolerance for clock/filesystem timestamp granularity -- confirmed necessary live, an exact >= check was flaky against a mocked instant test, though never a real concern in production where the subprocess call takes minutes). Treats exit-0-but-no-fresh-report as failure (return code 2), distinct from a genuine claude nonzero exit. 3 new/updated tests (fresh-report success path, garbled-output-despite-exit-0 failure, stale-report-doesn't-count), confirmed passing 3/3 consecutive runs after fixing the timing flakiness.

items.title: Windows Defender (MsMpEng.exe) + Docker Desktop likely causing real slowdowns/instability on this machine
items.action: Found 2026-08-30 while investigating a garbled weekly_code_audit.py run and a main.py catch-up run that appeared stuck on one step for a long stretch (both eventually completed -- confirmed slow, not truly deadlocked). Live process check: MsMpEng.exe (Windows Defender's real-time scanning engine) at ~206,949 CPU-seconds (~57.5 cumulative hours), com.docker.backend also consuming real CPU/memory in the background. Even lightweight, normally-instant tool calls (a repo-wide grep, ripgrep) took 20-120+ seconds or had to be backgrounded during this window. This looks like a genuine system-level resource contention problem -- likely Defender's real-time/on-access scanning reacting to the heavy file I/O this project's automation generates (git operations, log writes, multiple concurrent claude CLI subprocess invocations from a live session plus scheduled weekly audits plus background batch jobs) -- not a bug in any Leviathan script. This is the most plausible explanation for the same day's weekly_code_audit.py garbled-output incident (see weekly-code-audit-exit-code-not-proof-of-report) and WeeklyAudit's own reported ~10x-slower-than-baseline pytest run and denied/retried tool calls.
items.notes: NOT fixed -- modifying antivirus/security settings or Docker configuration is a system-settings change outside what should be done autonomously; flagging for the user's own decision. A common, standard mitigation worth considering: add a Windows Defender exclusion for the Leviathan project directory (and/or the python.exe / claude CLI executables) to stop real-time scanning from re-scanning this project's own heavy, repeated file I/O. Also worth considering: whether Docker Desktop needs to run continuously on this machine, or only when actually needed. No code action possible on this item from within the repo.

items.title: Resolve-First Top-N Per Bucket
items.action: User asked to expand scope on active bets to collect resolved_count data faster, without breaking core practices (many backlog gates -- calibration-curve n>=50, edge-decay-analysis n>=30, slippage-tracking fills>=20, per-wallet-track-record wallet>=10, auto-calibration-loop n>=30/per-category>=15 -- are stalled behind sample-size thresholds). Investigated analysis/resolve_first.py, the existing deliberately mechanical (HARD FREEZE: no new heuristic/scoring/calibration code) near-dated paper-bet logger built specifically for this purpose. Its select_near_dated() kept only the single highest-volume market per (price_band, flag_path) bucket -- a real ceiling of ~12 picks/day (4 bands x the 3 flag_path values actually reachable under the live flag_mode=strict_with_heuristic: DRIFT/HEURISTIC/None, not the full 5-value EDGE/BR_NONE/DRIFT/HEURISTIC/None set a naive estimate would assume), independent of how many near-dated markets are actually available.
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-31. Added a picks_per_bucket parameter to select_near_dated() (default 1, preserving exact prior behavior -- every pre-existing test/caller unaffected) that keeps the top N highest-volume candidates per bucket. Pure selection-cardinality change over already-computed heuristic outputs (flag_path/band come from scanner.score_markets(), called before this function, unmodified) -- no new judgment/scoring logic, so the file's own HARD FREEZE holds. New config key scoring.resolve_first_picks_per_bucket. 4 new tests (default-matches-prior, top-N-picks-N-highest-volume, never-fabricates-beyond-real-inventory, buckets-selected-independently), full suite green (2300 passed, 1 skipped). Live-verified against the real current snapshot the same day: N=1 (old default) selected 5 picks, N=3 selected 13 picks -- a genuine 2.6x increase, not a synthetic estimate -- with 0 filtered by the existing 7-day dedup safeguard (scoring.resolve_first_dedup_days, untouched). Set live to 3. See also near-dated-fetch-headroom-increase (companion change, same investigation) and trial-stronger-model-main-scoring (separate, unrelated lever from the same user request -- resolve_first.py never calls Claude at all, it uses scanner.score_markets()'s heuristic-only function).

items.title: Near-Dated Fetch Target/Page Budget Increase
items.action: Companion to resolve-first-top-n-per-bucket, same investigation. The near-dated fetch feeding both main.py's snapshot and resolve_first.py's candidate pool (core.kalshi.fetch_near_dated_markets(), config.json's markets.near_dated_target_count/near_dated_max_pages) was capped at 200/30. The existing near-dated-window-chunking backlog item's own notes already confirmed this was 'target hit' (i.e. real headroom exists beyond 200, not market scarcity) -- production logs across 3 separate runs all showed a clean, non-slow 200/200 fetch.
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-31 (Step A only, evidence-gated per this project's own discipline -- no Step B number pre-committed). Raised near_dated_target_count 200->300, near_dated_max_pages 30->40 in both config.json and config.example.json (with a _near_dated_notes update). Live-verified before touching the live config: a direct fetch_near_dated_markets(target_count=300, max_pages=40) call against the real Kalshi API returned the full 300 in 1.6 seconds -- far under Leviathan-ResolveFirst's 10-minute ExecutionTimeLimit, confirming real headroom rather than assuming it. Separately verified the wider fetch's real effect on resolve_first's candidate pool: a fresh near-dated-only fetch at the new target_count populated the previously-empty 60-95% price band (7 real candidates, was 0 under the old 200-target snapshot) and yielded 16 picks with picks_per_bucket=3, vs. 13 from the same day's combined-pipeline snapshot built under the old 200 target. Explicitly flagged: this fetch is shared with main.py's own snapshot pipeline, so the wider pool also feeds the main Claude-scored scanner before its own dedup_by_event/ranking runs -- a beneficial but distinct side effect from the resolve_first-specific lever above, not silently bundled. Step B (a further bump, e.g. 300->400) deliberately deferred pending a few real scheduled 8:30am runs' worth of observed timing, not set in advance. near_dated_max_days (14) and resolve_first_dedup_days (7) both left untouched.

items.title: Fix Dead --model Wiring in _score_via_cli
items.action: Second, independent lever from the same user request ('expand scope... collect data faster, use higher models'). core/scorer.py's _score_via_cli() -- the function the live pipeline actually uses (config.llm.backend defaults to 'cli') -- never passed a --model flag to the claude CLI subprocess. config.llm.model was completely dead for the live pipeline; it only ever fed the disabled metered-API backend (llm.api_spend_authorized=false by policy). 'Use higher models' wasn't wired up at all before this fix. Note: analysis/resolve_first.py never calls Claude (it uses scanner.score_markets(), the heuristic-only function) -- this lever only affects main.py's Claude-scored pass, entirely separate from the resolve-first-top-n-per-bucket/near-dated-fetch-headroom-increase levers above.
items.notes: RESOLVED 2026-08-31. Added config.llm.cli_model_override (new, distinct key, default null) rather than reusing the existing llm.model key -- that key holds "claude-sonnet-4-6", live-verified the same day to be STALER than the bare CLI's own current default (a bare `claude --print` with no --model flag resolves to claude-sonnet-5) -- wiring the old value through as-is would have been a silent downgrade, the opposite of the ask. When unset (the live default), --model is omitted entirely -- live-verified via a real CLI call with a captured-args spy that this produces the byte-identical argument list as before the change. When set, --model is appended with the exact configured value (confirmed both a short alias like 'opus' and the CLI's documented support for full model-id strings via `claude --help`). Threaded config through all 3 call sites in core/scorer.py (score_markets's single-pass and multi-sample paths, rescore_single_market) plus analysis/eval_rescore.py. 2 new tests (omits flag when unset across three unset-shapes, passes flag+value when set), full suite green. Live config.json left at cli_model_override=null -- this fix changes no default behavior; see trial-stronger-model-main-scoring for the separate, later decision to actually use it.

items.title: Bounded Trial: Stronger Model for Main Scoring Pass
items.action: Using the now-live config.llm.cli_model_override (see wire-llm-model-cli-flag, done -- no depends_on here since that item is already done as of this item's own creation, not a real gate), run a bounded 5-7 scheduled-run trial with a stronger model (e.g. 'opus') for main.py's Claude-scored pipeline only. Compare signal counts/pass-rates/edge distributions against the preceding baseline window, then revert the single config key back to null.
items.notes: Deliberately NOT executed as part of the wiring fix -- this is a separate, later go/no-go decision, not a default change. Real trade-off, live-verified 2026-08-31: a heavier model is slower per call and consumes more of the flat-rate Pro-plan usage/session budget, which could REDUCE how many markets are scorable per day -- directly cutting against the 'collect data faster' half of the original request even if per-call scoring quality improves. Direction of the quality effect (more genuine signals clearing thresholds vs. becoming more conservative and passing fewer) is unproven without this controlled test. If run: main.py's model_used report field currently sources from the separate, cosmetic scoring.scorer_model config key -- keep it manually in sync with whatever cli_model_override actually was for that run's window, or results will be misattributed to the wrong model in reporting.
